paras: The killing of John Spicy was the fatal shooting of a Black man, also named in the papers as Lucius Edmunds, by men sent to arrest him at or near Leary's, Georgia, in late September 1882. The telegraphic dispatch from Atlanta described a fight with a sheriff's posse in which Spicy wounded one of the posse and accidentally shot his wife before he was killed. The brief dispatch ran in papers from Washington to Seattle, while a later Georgia account gave a different, longer sequence of events.

According to the Savannah Morning News, Spicy was a fugitive from Dougherty County, where he was "charged with horse stealing." The same report said his wife, "on account of brutal treatment towards her," had a warrant issued for his arrest, and that officers Williams and Putman went to his house to serve it.

The wire dispatch, dated Atlanta, September 27, said that in a fight between Spicy and a sheriff's posse he was killed, after he "first shot one of the posse and accidentally shot his wife." Versions differed on her wound, calling it "probably," "perhaps" or plainly "fatally" inflicted. A syndicated weekly brief added that a deputy sheriff "was badly hurt."

The Savannah Morning News told the story in two stages. When the officers entered the house, it said, Spicy held his wife before him, shot Williams in the abdomen "without, however, doing serious harm," threw her against the officer and ran out the door as Putman fired a ball through his hat. On Monday morning about daylight, Spicy went into his yard when his dog barked, was ordered by someone to surrender, and fired at a man standing near the corner of his house. The unknown man then hit him with squirrel shot in the face and shoulder and, as he fell back against the house, with a load of buckshot in the abdomen and thigh; Spicy died the following Wednesday night.
No report of an inquest, arrest or official inquiry into the shooting appears in the coverage, and no later report of the wife's fate was found.

White papers across the country carried the Atlanta dispatch on September 27 and 28, usually as a single sentence among other crime news. Headline writers framed Spicy as the aggressor: "A Desperate Negro" in Seattle, "A Desperado Killed" in the Daily Globe, "Another Brawler Fired Out" in Rock Island and "Killed by a Sheriff's Posse" in the Washington Evening Star. The Wheeling Register headed it "Terrible Fight Between a Sheriff's Posse and a Negro," and the Cheyenne Daily Leader ran it as "Bloody Work."

The story kept circulating into October through weekly miscellany columns, including a German-language version in Der Nordstern of St. Cloud, Minnesota. The Bismarck Tribune reprinted the dispatch under the heading "An Alabama Fracas," though its text gave the Atlanta dateline. Only the Savannah Morning News, in its Georgia news column of October 3, supplied names of officers, the charges against Spicy and the account of his death in his yard; no paper commented editorially.

The wire compressed the events into one fight with a posse, while the Savannah account separated a failed arrest from a later shooting by a man it did not identify or connect to the officers. The dates also differ: the wire dispatch is dated September 27, whereas Savannah put the fatal shooting on a Monday and the death on a Wednesday night, and its opening line said he was killed "on last Thursday." The wire placed the fight at Leary's, but the Savannah report put it at Arlington.

reader.title: Killing of John Spicy
bases: The Atlanta wire reports a Black man killed in a fight with a sheriff's posse sent to arrest him (A2, A1); the Savannah Morning News account has officers attempt the arrest and an unidentified man fire the fatal shots (A26).

The Atlanta wire (A1, A2) and the separate, more detailed Georgia account in the Savannah Morning News (A26) agree that John Spicy was shot and killed while officers sought to arrest him, though they differ on sequence, place and who fired.

accounts.label: Atlanta wire dispatch from Leary's
accounts.gist: In a fight with a sheriff's posse, Edmunds, alias John Spicy, was killed; resisting, he shot one of the posse and accidentally shot his wife, perhaps or probably fatally.

accounts.label: Savannah Morning News Georgia news column
accounts.gist: Officers Williams and Putman came to serve the wife's warrant; Spicy shot Williams, using his wife as a shield, and fled; on Monday at daylight an unknown man in his yard shot him, and he died Wednesday night.

accounts.label: Syndicated weekly brief
accounts.gist: John Spicy was killed resisting arrest near Leary's on September 27; he fatally wounded his wife and a deputy sheriff was badly hurt.

framing.detail: Papers nationwide ran the Atlanta dispatch under headings like 'A Desperate Negro', 'A Desperado Killed', 'Another Brawler Fired Out' and 'A Negro Killed', taking the posse's account of resistance as fact.
The Savannah Morning News gave a fuller Georgia account in its state news column, relaying the allegations of horse stealing and brutal treatment without comment.
